Text:
Normal pulse rate in beats/min, by age group:

Neonate — {{c1::100 to 180}}

Infant — {{c1::100 to 160}}

Toddler — {{c1::90 to 150}}

Preschool age — {{c1::80 to 140}}

School age — {{c1::70 to 120}}

Adolescent through older adult — {{c1::60 to 100}}
Back Extra:
Pitfall: age cuts both ways — a neonate's ceiling of 180 beats/min is baseline rather than distress, while an older adult gets no allowance at all and is held to the same 60 to 100 as a 20-year-old.

Cue: the lower bound walks down in clean tens — 100 for the neonate and infant, then 90, 80, 70, and 60 from adolescence on.

visual_source.note: figure extracted from the source PDF and attached to this card (scripts/attach_figures.py --to-cards).

Text:
Normal respiratory rate in breaths/min, by age group:

Neonate — {{c1::30 to 60}}

Infant — {{c1::25 to 50}}

Toddler — {{c1::20 to 30}}

Preschool age — {{c1::20 to 25}}

School age — {{c1::15 to 20}}

Adolescent through older adult — {{c1::12 to 20}}
Back Extra:
Pitfall: an infant breathing 40 breaths/min is normal, but the identical rate in an adult is double the adult ceiling of 20 — a respiratory rate means nothing until the patient's age is known.

Cue: a neonate's slowest normal breathing, 30 breaths/min, is still faster than an adult's fastest normal, 20 — the two bands never overlap.

visual_source.note: figure extracted from the source PDF and attached to this card (scripts/attach_figures.py --to-cards).

Text:
Normal systolic blood pressure in mm Hg, by age group:

Neonate — {{c1::50 to 70}}

Infant — {{c1::70 to 95}}

Toddler and preschool age — {{c1::80 to 100}}

School age — {{c1::80 to 110}}

Adolescent — {{c1::90 to 110}}

Early, middle, and older adult — {{c1::90 to 130}}
Back Extra:
Distinguish: systolic pressure is the only one of the four vital signs that climbs with age — a neonate's floor of 50 mm Hg is little more than half the adult floor of 90.

Pitfall: an adolescent reaches adult pulse and respiratory values but not adult pressure — the systolic ceiling holds at 110 until age 19, then rises to 130.

visual_source.note: figure extracted from the source PDF and attached to this card (scripts/attach_figures.py --to-cards).

Text:
Normal body temperature by age group:

Neonate — {{c1::98°F to 100°F (37°C to 38°C)}}

Infant and toddler — {{c1::96.8°F to 99.6°F (36°C to 37.5°C)}}

Preschool age through older adult — {{c1::98.6°F (37°C)}}
Back Extra:
Distinguish: temperature is the one vital sign with no steady climb or fall across the age groups — its own band for the first three years, then a fixed 98.6°F (37°C) from preschool age onward.

Cue: the neonate is the only group whose normal reaches 100°F (38°C), and the infant and toddler are the only ones whose normal dips below 98°F.

visual_source.note: figure extracted from the source PDF and attached to this card (scripts/attach_figures.py --to-cards).

Text:
The nine life-span age groups and the ages each one covers:

Neonate — {{c1::birth to 1 month}}

Infant — {{c1::1 month to 1 year}}

Toddler — {{c1::1 to 3 years}}

Preschool age — {{c1::3 to 6 years}}

School age — {{c1::6 to 12 years}}

Adolescent — {{c1::12 to 18 years}}

Early adult — {{c1::19 to 40 years}}

Middle adult — {{c1::41 to 60 years}}

Older adult — {{c1::61 years and older}}
Back Extra:
Why: no other phase of life changes as fast as the first year, which is why those 12 months alone carry two names — neonate for the first month, infant for the remaining eleven.

Pitfall: the childhood bands share a boundary year, so one age can sit in two groups — a 12-year-old is both school age and adolescent — while the adult bands do not overlap, since adolescence ends at 18 and early adulthood starts at 19.

visual_source.note: figure extracted from the source PDF and attached to this card (scripts/attach_figures.py --to-cards).

Text: As a person gets older, pulse rate and respiratory rate {{c1::decrease::increase or decrease}}, whereas systolic blood pressure tends to {{c1::increase::increase or decrease}}.
Back Extra:
Pitfall: the climb has a ceiling — systolic pressure stops rising once it reaches 90 to 130 in early adulthood and is identical in middle and older adults, so a high reading in a 70-year-old is a finding, not an age effect.

Cue: the same 70 mm Hg that is an infant's healthy floor sits 20 mm Hg below the adult floor of 90 — which is exactly why the ranges have to be age-banded at all.

visual_source.note: TABLE 7-1 'Vital Signs at Various Ages' — caption on p683, body is a rendered image on p684 with no text layer. Every value on this card was read off the extracted plate work/emt/figures/TABLE_7_1.png.

Text: A pulse of 140 beats/min is a {{c1::normal::normal or life-threatening}} finding in an infant, but the same rate in a 30-year-old adult signals a {{c1::life-threatening::normal or life-threatening}} condition.
Back Extra:
Why: 140 beats/min sits inside the infant's normal 100 to 160 but runs 40 beats/min past the adult ceiling of 100 — a vital sign has no meaning until the patient's age is known.

Pitfall: the trap runs both ways — a pulse of 70 beats/min is unremarkable in an adult but dangerously slow in a neonate, whose normal starts at 100.
verified_by: p683 prose, verbatim: "Finding a pulse rate of 140 beats/min ... is usually normal for an infant. However, for a 30-year-old adult, the same values would likely signal the presence of a life-threatening condition." Corroborated on the rendered plate figures/TABLE_7_1.png: infant pulse 100 to 160 (140 inside), adult pulse 60 to 100 (140 far outside), neonate pulse floor 100. The prose's companion figure of 60 breaths/min was REMOVED by the editor: TABLE 7-1 caps infant respirations at 50 and puts 60 only in the neonate band, so the book contradicts itself on that digit.

visual_source.note: figure extracted from the source PDF and attached to this card (scripts/attach_figures.py --to-cards).

Text:
A neonate's body weight follows a predictable course:

At birth: {{c1::6 to 8 lb (3 to 3.5 kg)}}

First week: falls {{c1::5% to 10%}} from fluid loss

Second week onward: gains about {{c1::1 ounce (30 g) per day}}

Doubles birth weight by {{c1::4 to 6 months}}

Triples birth weight by {{c1::1 year}}
Back Extra:
Ex: a 7 lb newborn is about 14 lb at 6 months and about 21 lb at 1 year.

Pitfall: doubling and tripling are multiples of the birth weight, not of whatever the infant weighs at the time.

visual_source.note: figure extracted from the source PDF and attached to this card (scripts/attach_figures.py --to-cards).

Text: A neonate's head accounts for about {{c1::25%}} of total body weight, which is why neonates and infants tend to land {{c2::headfirst}} when they fall.
Back Extra:
Why: the risk of head injury is compounded by an infant's inability to extend the arms to cushion or slow a fall.

Pitfall: keep head and spinal trauma high on the index of suspicion after any fall by a neonate or infant.

Text: Neonates are primarily {{c1::nose::nose or mouth}} breathers, and infants younger than {{c2::6 months::age}} are especially susceptible to congestion that can lead to viral upper respiratory infections.
Back Extra:
Distinguish: nose breathing is described for the neonate and the heightened susceptibility to nasal congestion runs through the first 6 months, so in a young infant a blocked nose is an airway problem, not just a stuffy nose.

Why: an infant who breathes through the nose has no easy second route, so even mucus can compromise ventilation.

Text: You are dispatched for a 2-month-old who is reportedly choking. The mouth and throat are clear, yet the infant is still struggling to breathe, so you check next for obstruction of {{c1::the nasal passages::anatomic site}}.
Back Extra:
Why: neonates and young infants breathe primarily through the nose, so mucus alone can present as a choking emergency.

Pitfall: susceptibility to nasal congestion runs through the first 6 months, so a reported choking in this age group is often a blocked nose.

Text:
Airway obstruction is more common in infants than in older children and adults. Compared with an adult, what is anatomically different about an infant's airway and head?

{{c1::a larger tongue relative to the size of the oral cavity}}

{{c1::a proportionally shorter and narrower airway}}

{{c1::a proportionally oversized occiput}}

{{c1::a more flexible trachea}}
Back Extra:
Cue: name what is bigger (the tongue and the occiput), what is smaller (the airway), and what is floppier (the trachea).

Why: the oversized occiput, the flexible trachea, and an infant's limited ability to reposition are why the EMT must protect airway patency through proper positioning.

Text: In an infant, the EMT preserves airway patency through proper positioning, because both {{c1::hyperextending}} and {{c1::hyperflexing}} the head and neck can easily produce an airway obstruction.
Back Extra:
Meaning: hyperextension tips the head too far back, and hyperflexion lets the chin drop toward the chest.

Why: an infant has limited or absent ability to reposition, so whatever head and neck position the EMT sets is the one the infant stays in.

Text: An infant's rib cage is {{c1::less::more or less}} rigid and the ribs sit {{c1::horizontally::orientation}}, which explains the {{c2::diaphragmatic (belly) breathing}} typically seen in infants.
Back Extra: Pitfall: belly breathing is the normal pattern for an infant, so abdominal movement by itself is not a sign of distress.

Text: {{c1::Barotrauma}} is {{c2::pressure-induced trauma to the lungs}}, and in an infant the cause is {{c3::forceful ventilations and overinflation}} with a bag-mask.
Back Extra:
Why: an infant's lungs are fragile, the breathing muscles are immature, and the alveoli are relatively few.

Pitfall: an infant's oxygen need is low but a stressed infant compensates poorly, so extra force adds risk without adding benefit.

Text:
In a healthy, full-term newborn, four reflexes are present at birth:

{{c1::Moro (startle)}}

{{c1::palmar grasp}}

{{c1::rooting}}

{{c1::sucking}}
Back Extra:
Ex: an object placed in the newborn's palm makes the hand close around it — that is the palmar grasp; stroking the lips prompts the baby to latch on — that is the sucking reflex.

Cue: rooting and sucking are the two reflexes that serve feeding.

Text:
Name the newborn reflex from how it presents:

The arms fly open wide and the fingers spread, as if grabbing at something = the {{c1::Moro}} reflex

Something touches the cheek and the head turns toward the touch = the {{c1::rooting}} reflex
Back Extra:
Cue: the Moro reflex is more often called the startle reflex.

Why: the newborn nervous system is well established at birth but not yet mature, which is why a healthy, full-term infant already produces these responses reliably.

Text: {{c1::Fontanelles::structures}} are the {{c2::flexible fibrous gaps between cranial bones}}, and they let the newborn's head {{c3::change shape}} as it passes through the narrow birth canal.
Back Extra: Why: in the months after birth the cranial bones grow together and fuse into a unified, rigid structure, so a fontanelle is a temporary finding.

visual_source.note: figure extracted from the source PDF and attached to this card (scripts/attach_figures.py --to-cards).

Text:
The fontanelles do not close at the same age:

Posterior fontanelle → closes by {{c1::the third month}}

Anterior fontanelle → closes between {{c1::9 and 18 months}}
Back Extra: Cue: the anterior fontanelle stays open far longer than the posterior one, so beyond early infancy it is the only fontanelle left to assess.

visual_source.note: figure extracted from the source PDF and attached to this card (scripts/attach_figures.py --to-cards).

Text: In an infant with an open fontanelle, a {{c1::depressed::depressed or bulging}} fontanelle may indicate {{c2::dehydration}}, whereas a {{c1::bulging::depressed or bulging}} fontanelle often signals {{c2::increased intracranial pressure}}.
Back Extra:
Mnemonic: a sunken fontanelle is a low tank — think fluid loss.

Pitfall: a fontanelle reads this way only while it is still open, so the sign is gone once it has closed.

visual_source.note: figure extracted from the source PDF and attached to this card (scripts/attach_figures.py --to-cards).

Text: Teething (baby teeth breaking through the gums) can be {{c1::painful}} and is sometimes accompanied by a {{c1::low-grade}} fever.
Back Extra: Pitfall: teething accounts only for a low-grade fever, so a higher fever in an infant is not explained by teething.

Text:
Match each characteristic to the age at which it typically appears in an infant:

Reaches arms out to people; drools → {{c1::4 months}}

Sleeps throughout the night; distinguishes family members from strangers → {{c1::5 months}}

Recognizes familiar faces; uses the eyes to track objects and people → {{c1::2 months}}

Begins teething; sits upright; speaks one-syllable words → {{c1::6 months}}

Brings objects to the mouth; smiles and frowns → {{c1::3 months}}
Back Extra:
Distinguish: bringing objects to the mouth is the 3-month characteristic, while deliberately exploring objects by placing them in the mouth comes months later; in the same way, sitting upright at 6 months precedes sitting alone.

Cue: the first half-year develops outward from the eyes, running recognizing and tracking first, then the hands and mouth (reaching, drooling, mouthing), then the trunk and the first one-syllable words.

Text:
Match each infant characteristic to the age at which it typically appears:

Pulls self up to stand; explores objects by placing them in the mouth → {{c1::9 months}}

Knows his or her name; walks → {{c1::12 months}}

Afraid of strangers; displays mood swings → {{c1::7 months}}

Begins to walk without assistance; becomes frustrated by restrictions → {{c1::11 months}}

Responds to "no"; can sit alone; plays peek-a-boo → {{c1::8 months}}

Responds to his or her name; crawls efficiently → {{c1::10 months}}
Back Extra:
Distinguish: two look-alike pairs split by degree. An infant responds to his or her name at 10 months but knows it at 12, and begins to walk without assistance at 11 months but simply walks at 12.

Cue: the second half-year is one long mobility ladder, sitting alone, then pulling up to stand, then crawling, then walking, and it opens with the social shift at 7 months when the infant first becomes afraid of strangers.

Text: In older infants, {{c1::separation anxiety}} is common, marked by {{c2::clingy behavior}} and {{c2::fear of unfamiliar places and people}}, and typically peaking between {{c3::10 and 18 months}} of age.
Back Extra:
Distinguish: an infant who instead shows little emotional response to a caregiver and treats that caregiver like a stranger is showing anxious-avoidant attachment, which results from recurring rejection.

Cue: crying as a means of protest is normal at this age, so an infant who clings and cries when a parent steps out of the room is behaving as expected.

Text: The psychosocial stage of {{c1::trust versus mistrust}} begins at {{c2::birth}} and concludes at approximately {{c2::18 months}} of age.
Back Extra:
Meaning: trust versus mistrust is the stretch of infancy in which children learn whether the people around them can be relied on.

Mechanism: infants depend entirely on their caregivers, so the crucial element is the quality of care. Needs met consistently in a stable environment build trust, while caregivers who are inconsistent, emotionally unavailable, or rejecting build mistrust.

Pitfall: an environment too unpredictable for the infant can trigger despair and withdrawal, and the resulting trust issues may surface later in life.

visual_source.note: figure extracted from the source PDF and attached to this card (scripts/attach_figures.py --to-cards).

Text: A toddler's and preschooler's lungs keep adding terminal bronchioles and alveoli, but the {{c1::musculature}} of those lungs is still poorly developed, so they cannot sustain {{c2::deep or rapid respirations::breathing pattern}} for long.
Back Extra:
Why: the extra terminal bronchioles and alveoli are being added to meet a growing body's ever-increasing oxygen demand.

Pitfall: the ceiling is muscular, not structural — a hard-breathing toddler runs out of power, not out of gas-exchange surface.

Text: In toddlers the loss of {{c1::passive immunity}} plus constant exposure to other children brings frequent viral colds, which often show up as {{c2::upper respiratory symptoms}} or {{c2::gastrointestinal distress}}. The antibodies those repeated infections generate become {{c3::acquired immunity}}.
Back Extra:
Why: the loss of passive immunity is called out as one of the most important physiologic changes of the toddler years, and it lands exactly when the child starts spending time around other children.

Distinguish: passive immunity is the protection the toddler is losing; acquired immunity is what replaces it.

Text: By the end of the preschooler stage, a child's brain weighs roughly {{c1::90%::percentage}} of its adult weight.
Back Extra:
Cue: the preschool brain is nearly finished growing — the same stage in which play shifts from purely gross motor (grabbing an object with the whole palm) to fine motor (picking up a crayon with thumb and forefinger).

Distinguish: the preschooler stage runs 3 to 6 years, so the brain is near adult weight well before the body is anywhere close.

Text: Toddlers have the neuromuscular ability to control the bladder by {{c1::12 to 15 months::age range}}, but many are not psychologically ready for toilet training until {{c2::18 to 30 months::age range}}. On average, toilet training is complete at {{c3::28 months::age}}.
Back Extra:
Why: toilet training is the outward sign of renal-system maturation and the establishing of elimination patterns.

Cue: alongside speech development, it is one of the milestones by which a toddler wins the self-sufficiency at stake in the autonomy-versus-shame-and-doubt stage.

Text: Most children have mastered basic language skills by the age of {{c1::36 months::age}}, and understand full sentences by {{c2::3 or 4 years::age}}.
Back Extra: Cue: once the basics are in place, language stops being only a tool for asking for what they want and starts being used creatively and playfully.

visual_source.note: figure extracted from the source PDF and attached to this card (scripts/attach_figures.py --to-cards).

Text: Toddlers begin to understand the concept of cause and effect at about {{c1::18 to 24 months::age range}}.
Back Extra:
Cue: cause-and-effect lands in the same stretch as this age group's social gains — becoming more interactive with other children is what teaches a toddler to control their own behavior, follow rules, and be competitive.

Ex: by observing their role models, toddlers of this age also learn to recognize gender differences.

Text: You are treating a severely injured child when the father, overwhelmed by fear, begins to panic and can no longer answer your questions. On this call the father has become a {{c1::secondary patient::role on scene}}.
Back Extra:
Cue: on any call for a severely sick or injured child, look for the second patient on scene — a parent.

Pitfall: the parent's distress adds to an already intense situation and makes the task of treating the child much more difficult.

Text: Each year a school-age child gains about {{c1::4 pounds (2 kg)::weight}} and grows about {{c2::2.5 inches (6 cm)::height}}.
Back Extra: Cue: the same 6-to-12 stretch also swaps baby teeth for permanent teeth and brings a significant rise in brain activity in both hemispheres.

Text:
School-age children develop moral reasoning in three levels, each answering to a different influence:

{{c1::Preconventional}} → {{c2::external forces such as parental discipline}}

{{c1::Conventional}} → {{c2::the approval of peers and society}}

{{c1::Postconventional}} → {{c2::an internalized moral compass (conscience)}}
Back Extra:
Distinguish: under preconventional reasoning an act is right or wrong by its consequences — punishment or incentive. Conventional reasoning still accepts the rules of authority figures, but now because those rules are seen as necessary for positive relationships and acceptance. Postconventional reasoning turns abstract and answers to conscience alone.

Cue: the order tracks who is in charge — the punisher, then the group, then the self. Postconventional reasoning keeps developing through adolescence.

Text: {{c1::Self-concept}} is {{c2::our perception of ourselves}}, whereas {{c1::self-esteem}} is {{c2::how we feel about ourselves}} and how we fit in with our peers.
Back Extra:
Distinguish: self-concept is the picture you hold of yourself; self-esteem is the verdict on that picture.

Cue: both begin to take shape during the school-age years, the same stage in which the three levels of moral reasoning develop.

Text:
The adolescent growth spurt lasts {{c2::2 to 3 years::duration}} and proceeds in a fixed order:

{{c1::hands and feet}} → {{c1::long bones of the extremities}} → {{c1::torso}}
Back Extra:
Cue: growth runs periphery-inward — the parts farthest from the trunk enlarge first, and the trunk finishes last.

Why: the spurt is what brings the body to adult size — by its end, muscle mass and bone density have nearly reached adult levels.

visual_source.note: figure extracted from the source PDF and attached to this card (scripts/attach_figures.py --to-cards).

Text: Girls finish the adolescent growth spurt by about {{c1::16 years}}, whereas boys typically reach their growth peak by {{c1::18 years}} and generally become {{c1::taller::taller or shorter}} than girls.
Back Extra:
Why: girls enter the growth spurt at an earlier age than boys, so they finish sooner even though boys ultimately grow taller.

Pitfall: finishing by about 16 years ends the growth spurt, not adolescence, which runs 12 to 18 years.

visual_source.note: figure extracted from the source PDF and attached to this card (scripts/attach_figures.py --to-cards).

Text: The adolescent milestone called {{c1::menarche}} is {{c2::the first menstrual bleeding}}, and reaching it before the adolescent years is {{c3::not uncommon::uncommon or not uncommon}}.
Back Extra:
Pitfall: a girl who is already menstruating may still be younger than 12, so menarche does not confirm she has reached adolescence.

Why: menarche signals the maturing reproductive system — by the middle of adolescence the body gains the capacity for reproduction, producing sperm in males and eggs (oocytes) in females.

Ex: the other secondary sexual developments of adolescence are enlargement of the external reproductive organs, pubic and axillary hair, vocal changes, and adipose deposits in the breasts and thighs.

Text:
The leading cause of death changes with age:

All age groups younger than 44 years → {{c1::unintentional injury}}

Ages 45 to 64 years → {{c2::cancer}}, not heart disease
Back Extra:
Distinguish: the under-44 figure lumps all those ages together — for neonates and infants specifically, this chapter gives the leading cause of death as congenital abnormalities (birth defects).

Pitfall: middle adults may already have diabetes or hypertension without knowing it, so a denied medical history does not rule them out.

Cue: rising cholesterol, decreasing cardiac efficiency, and harder weight control mark these years, though proper exercise and a healthy diet blunt much of the effect.

Text: Cardiac function declines with age largely because of {{c1::atherosclerosis::vascular condition}}, a buildup of {{c2::cholesterol and calcium::two substances}} along the inner walls of blood vessels that forms plaque.
Back Extra: Mechanism: as plaque accumulates, blood flow through the affected vessels becomes restricted or blocked entirely.

Text: More than {{c1::60%::percentage}} of people older than {{c1::65 years::age}} have atherosclerotic disease.
Back Extra:
Distinguish: the age-related drop in heart rate is a baseline change, and the older adult's normal range is still 60 to 100 — the decrease is a drift within that band, not a lower normal. In a life-threatening illness the body still raises the heart rate to preserve blood pressure.

Pitfall: because cardiac muscle weakens with age, that faster rate may damage the heart, and combined with atherosclerosis of sufficient severity the damage could prove fatal.

visual_source.note: figure extracted from the source PDF and attached to this card (scripts/attach_figures.py --to-cards).

Text:
Beyond atherosclerosis, aging weakens the older adult's heart in three ways:

{{c1::the heart rate decreases}}

{{c1::cardiac output declines}}

{{c1::the ability to increase cardiac output on demand diminishes}}
Back Extra:
Distinguish: the age-related drop in heart rate is a baseline change, and the older adult's normal range is still 60 to 100 — the decrease is a drift within that band, not a lower normal. In a life-threatening illness the body still raises the heart rate to preserve blood pressure.

Meaning: cardiac output is the amount of blood pumped by the heart each minute.

Why: the aging heart is left less able to cope with exercise or disease.

Text: Because the older adult's vascular system stiffens, blood vessels cannot dilate and contract effectively, so {{c1::diastolic::systolic or diastolic}} blood pressure {{c1::increases::increases or decreases}} and the heart must work harder against vascular resistance.
Back Extra: Pitfall: over time the increased workload can be detrimental to the heart itself, so stiff vessels are a slow-building cardiac problem, not just a blood pressure reading.

Text: Human blood cells originate in the bone marrow, but with advancing age that marrow is replaced by {{c1::fatty tissue}}.
Back Extra:
Why: losing marrow means losing the ability to manufacture new blood cells.

Pitfall: alone the change is not cause for alarm, but in a traumatic injury where a large volume of blood is lost quickly, the impeded ability to replace those cells can be devastating.

Text:
Classify each of the four ways aging changes the older adult's respiratory system:

Size of the airway: {{c1::increases::increases or decreases}}

Surface area of the alveoli: {{c1::decreases::increases or decreases}}

Elasticity of the lungs: {{c1::decreases::increases or decreases}}

Strength of the intercostal muscles and diaphragm: {{c1::decreases::increases or decreases}}
Back Extra:
Why: smaller alveolar surface, stiffer lungs, and weaker breathing muscles together make breathing more laborious for the older adult.

Cue: three of the four go down with age — the size of the airway is the lone item that goes up.

Text: {{c1::Vital capacity}} is the volume of air moved during {{c2::the deepest inspiration and expiration}}.
Back Extra: Pitfall: the age-related respiratory changes are gradual and usually go unnoticed, until a severe, life-threatening illness makes the lack of respiratory reserve pronounced.

Text: By age {{c1::75::age}}, an older adult's vital capacity has declined to about {{c1::50%::percentage}} of that of a young adult.
Back Extra:
Distinguish: several aging declines land near half, so anchor this one to the lungs and to age 75 — intestinal blood flow and renal filtration each fall by up to 50% as well.

Pitfall: the aging chest is also more rigid yet more fragile — instead of bending and flexing under stress, the calcified rib cage is more susceptible to fracture.

Text:
With age, five protective features of the upper airway weaken:

{{c1::the cough reflex}}

{{c1::the gag reflex}}

{{c1::the ability to clear secretions}}

{{c1::the cilia that line the airway}}

{{c1::sensation within the airway}}
Back Extra: Why: losing all five at once is what makes an open upper airway hard to maintain in the older adult.

Text: As the structures protecting the upper airway lose function with age, the older adult is at greater risk of {{c1::aspiration}} and {{c1::airway obstruction}}.
Back Extra: Pitfall: the danger is a quiet one — the defenses that would normally alert the older adult and clear the airway fade together, so material can sit in the airway without obvious distress.

Text: With age, taste buds become less sensitive to {{c1::salty}} and {{c1::sweet}} foods, and food may be perceived as bland and flavorless because the sense of {{c2::smell}} fades along with taste.
Back Extra:
Why: dulled flavor is one of the age-related changes in gastric and intestinal function that together inhibit nutritional intake and utilization.

Ex: tooth loss makes chewing harder, decreased saliva impairs the breakdown of complex carbohydrates, and gastric acid secretion diminishes.

Text: {{c1::Peristalsis}} is the process in which intestinal contractions {{c2::move food along the digestive tract}}, and with age it {{c3::slows::speeds up or slows}}.
Back Extra: Pitfall: the aging gut changes in more ways than its speed — gallstones become increasingly common, and a less elastic anal sphincter can lead to fecal incontinence.

Text: Age-related change in peristalsis leaves an older adult prone to {{c1::constipation::bowel}} and/or {{c1::suppressed feelings of hunger::appetite}}.
Back Extra:
Pitfall: constipation and a poor appetite in an older adult are easy to write off as habit or mood, when one normal age change in the gut produces both.

Distinguish: appetite loss from peristalsis is a gut-motility effect, separate from the fading smell and taste that makes food seem bland.

Text: In older adults, blood flow to the intestines can drop by as much as {{c1::50%}}, so the extraction of {{c2::vitamins}} and {{c2::minerals}} from digested food wanes.
Back Extra:
Distinguish: the 50% belongs to intestinal blood flow, not to the renal figures for kidney size and filtration — keep each number tied to its organ.

Why: absorption depends on perfusion, so an older adult can take in enough food and still absorb fewer vitamins and minerals from it.

Text: Between the ages of 20 and 90 years, the kidneys decrease in size by {{c1::20%}} and their filtration capabilities decline by as much as {{c1::50%}}.
Back Extra:
Why: blood supply to the nephrons falls, and the number of nephrons itself declines between the ages of 30 and 80 years.

Pitfall: do not swap the two numbers. The 20% is anatomic (a smaller kidney) and the up-to-50% is functional (less filtering).

Text: Aging reduces renal function in two ways: the kidneys become less able to {{c1::remove waste}} from the body and less able to {{c1::conserve fluids}} when needed.
Back Extra:
Mechanism: the kidney filters blood inside its nephrons, and aging both shrinks their blood supply and reduces their number.

Pitfall: the fluid-conservation half is the one that gets forgotten, so an older adult who is losing volume also struggles to hold on to what is left.

Text: By the time a person is {{c1::80}} years of age, the brain has decreased in weight by as much as {{c2::10% to 20%}}.
Back Extra:
Why: motor and sensory neural networks become slower and less responsive over the same span of years.

Distinguish: an infant brain holds more neurons than an adult brain, yet the adult brain is far more flexible, because the number of interconnections between neurons increases with age.

Text: In an older adult, the brain's metabolic rate and oxygen consumption remain {{c1::unchanged::increased, decreased, or unchanged}}.
Back Extra:
Distinguish: aging changes the speed of the brain's neural networks, not its metabolic demand — motor and sensory networks become slower and less responsive while oxygen use holds steady.

Pitfall: a lighter, slower older brain is not a less oxygen-hungry one.

Text: In an older adult, age-related {{c1::shrinkage}} of the brain opens a void between the brain and the outermost layer of the meninges, so a rapid or forceful shift of the brain can tear the {{c2::bridging veins}}.
Back Extra:
Distinguish: at every other age the cranial vault is almost entirely occupied by the brain, the meningeal layers, and the cerebrospinal fluid between them, so there is virtually no empty space.

Mechanism: the void gives the brain room to move inside the cranium, which is the step that turns a rapid or forceful shift into a torn vein.

Text: An 82-year-old struck her head on a cabinet door and is alert with no complaints. In an older adult, bleeding around the brain after a head impact {{c1::may go unnoticed for some time::how it presents}}.
Back Extra:
Pitfall: a normal exam soon after a head impact does not clear an older patient, because blood can accumulate quietly in the space that opens around an aging brain.

Mechanism: the bleeding runs into that open space instead of pressing against a tightly packed cranial vault, which is why the signs arrive late.
